# Explain a tricky school topic with Grok in five minutes

> **In short:** Open Grok, name the topic and your child's age, and ask it to retell the subject as a short story. You'll have a simple, kid-friendly explanation in about a minute, ready to read together at the kitchen table.

Homework time can go from calm to chaos in about ten minutes flat — usually the moment a tricky word appears in the textbook and nobody in the room can explain it. Grok is an AI assistant made by xAI, and one of the things it does well is take a confusing subject and rewrite it as a story a kid can actually follow. You don't need to be a teacher. You just need to know the topic, the age, and a good opening message. One honest note up front: Grok can rewrite the topic as a story, but it can't replace reading the textbook or doing the actual homework — your child still needs to know what the teacher is asking for.

## Before you start
- A Grok account — you can sign up at the official Grok site or inside the X app. The basic chat is usually available on the free plan; some newer or more powerful models may need a paid tier, so check the current plan list if you want the strongest answer.
- A phone, tablet or computer with Grok open in a browser or app.
- The exact homework topic from your child's book, worksheet or class note — even a rough idea works.
- About **5–7 minutes** total.

## Step 1 — Open Grok and start a new chat
Open the Grok app on your phone, or visit grok.com in a browser on your computer. Look for the **chat box near the bottom of the screen** — usually a rounded text field labeled something like "Ask anything" or "Message Grok." If you've used Grok before, your old chats appear in a sidebar on the web or behind a menu icon on mobile. Tap the **"New chat"** button or the **pencil / "+" icon** to start fresh, so the assistant doesn't get confused by an earlier conversation.
💬 Example: tap the "+" or pencil icon at the top of the chat list to open a blank chat.
If your screen looks different, the new-chat option is often hidden behind a **☰ menu** at the top-left, or inside an account/profile icon at the top-right — open it and look for a "New chat" entry.
You'll know it worked when you see a blank chat screen with a single text field and no old messages above it.

## Step 2 — Name the topic, the age and the goal
Type one clear sentence into the chat box that includes three things: the subject (for example, "the water cycle" or "the French Revolution"), your child's age or grade, and what you want — usually "as a short story" or "in simple words." Then press the **paper-plane icon ➤** or hit **Return / Enter** to send. Grok starts typing a reply within a few seconds; you'll see words appear one by one, the way a person would text.
💬 Example: *"My son is 10. Please explain the water cycle as a short story he can read on his own — about 150 words, no big words."*
If your screen shows a **microphone icon** instead of a text box, tap the small **keyboard icon** to switch to typing first. Some mobile builds put the new-chat option behind the **☰ menu** — open it and choose "New chat" if you skipped Step 1.
You'll know it worked when Grok starts writing a response — usually a title line, then a paragraph or two of story text.

## Step 3 — Ask for one small example or scene
Stories land better when there's a concrete moment the child can picture in their head. After the first reply, send a short follow-up asking Grok to add **one tiny example, analogy or scene** — something a kid can see (a leaf, a king, a battery, a fish). This makes the idea stick. Type it the same way: into the text box, then tap the send arrow. Grok rewrites or extends the explanation in plain English.
💬 Example: *"Can you add one short scene with a leaf falling off a tree, so the 'evaporation' part makes sense?"*
If the reply feels too long or too grown-up, just say so — *"A bit shorter, please, and use simpler words."* The assistant adjusts in the next message. If the text field won't send, check that you didn't accidentally tap a microphone, and that the message bubble actually appears above the chat box.
You'll know it worked when the new reply contains a concrete image your child can repeat back to you — "a leaf falls into a puddle and floats up as steam."

## Step 4 — Read it together and ask one question
Sit with your child and read the story out loud — slowly is fine. Pause at the end and ask **one** question to check the idea landed. You can type it into Grok first to see if the assistant agrees with the answer, or ask your child directly and then check together. This is where homework stops being a fight: your child is retelling, not being quizzed.
💬 Example: ask your child *"So what does the sun do to the water in the puddle?"* — then type *"Did I explain the water cycle correctly to a 10-year-old?"* into Grok for a sanity check.
If Grok's answer comes back with new vocabulary your child doesn't know, ask it to **swap the hard word for a friendlier one** — *"Replace the word 'precipitation' with something a 10-year-old would actually say."* If your child loses interest halfway, ask Grok to **shrink the story** to about 80 words and try again.
You'll know it worked when your child can summarize the topic in their own words without staring at the textbook.

## Step 5 — Save the story for next time
If the topic is going to come up again — most school subjects do — keep the chat. Look for a **"Share" or "Copy" icon** near Grok's reply, often a small arrow pointing up or two overlapping squares. Tap it to copy the text into a notes app, an email or a message to yourself. That way, tomorrow's homework — or next week's review — starts with a story your child already half-remembers.
💬 Example: tap the share icon, then paste the story into Apple Notes, Google Keep or a simple text message to yourself.
If you don't see a share button, **long-press the reply text on mobile** (or **right-click on a computer**) and choose **"Copy"** — the text goes to your clipboard, ready to paste anywhere. Inside the X app, the chat lives within X itself, so saving usually means copying the story out before you close the tab.
You'll know it worked when the story is safely in your notes app, ready to open at the kitchen table tomorrow.

## Common mistakes
- **Asking for "an explanation" without naming the age.** Grok will write for an adult, and the child will tune out. Always include the age in the very first message.
- **Treating the first reply as the final one.** A great explanation usually takes two or three short follow-ups. If it feels off, ask Grok to try again in simpler words — don't give up after one round.
- **Quizzing instead of retelling.** Asking "did you understand?" puts a child on the spot. Asking "tell it back to me in your own words" is much kinder and shows whether the story actually landed.

## What this means for you
- **In everyday life:** the next time a homework page makes everyone in the room sigh, you can turn it into a five-minute story instead of a thirty-minute argument.
- **For your business or work:** the same trick — *"explain X like I'm 10"* — is one of the fastest ways to break down a dense report, a contract clause or a long email you don't fully understand.
- **If you're just getting started:** start with one subject your child already half-likes — a favorite animal, a sport, a video game world — and ask Grok to explain it in story form. It's the easiest first win.

## Try it now
Pick one topic from tonight's homework, open Grok, and paste this: *"My child is 10. Please explain [TOPIC] as a 150-word story with no big words. End with one tiny example."* Read the result together and see how it lands.
